Adult Atlantic Spanish mackerel typically attain a maximum fork length of 91 centimeters [Li = 91 centimeters], making them one of the larger scombrids in the western Atlantic. The body mass associated with this ultimate size can be substantial; individuals approaching the asymptotic length generally weigh roughly 6.55 kilograms [Wwi = roughly 6.55 kilograms], though this estimate derives from length-weight relationships and shows some seasonal variation. Females begin preparing for reproduction once they reach a fork length of approximately 40.5 centimeters [Lp = approximately 40.5 centimeters], although strong regional differences exist, with populations in the Gulf of Mexico reaching this size threshold earlier than those along the northeastern seaboard. At puberty, the typical body mass is about 568 grams [Wwp = about 568 grams], a value that reflects the substantial energetic investment required to support the transition to a reproductive life history. This pattern of delayed maturity is characteristic of fast-growing, medium-lived pelagic predators.

The reproductive biology of Atlantic Spanish mackerel is notable for its high potential output. Under favorable environmental conditions, particularly at water temperatures around 24.1 °C [T = 24.1 °C], females produce an average of 5754 eggs per day [Ri = an average of 5754 eggs per day], a figure that represents the maximum daily reproductive rate observed in field populations. This rate is calculated by dividing the total seasonal fecundity by the number of spawning days, reflecting a strategy of batch spawning that spreads reproductive effort across several months. The pelagic eggs, each with an average diameter of approximately 1 millimeter, are released during multiple spawning events that coincide with warm surface temperatures and abundant planktonic prey for the resulting larvae. This high fecundity compensates for the substantial mortality experienced during the early life stages.

Egg development proceeds rapidly in this species. Larvae emerge from the chorion approximately 1.02 days [ab = approximately 1.02 days] after fertilization when incubation temperatures are maintained at 25.5 °C [T = 25.5 °C], a thermal regime typical of late spring and summer spawning grounds. The yolk-sac larva, initially measuring just a few millimeters in total length, weighs approximately 0.00052 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00052 grams] at the moment of hatching, reflecting the tiny but yolk-rich egg from which it emerges. This brief embryonic period allows the species to exploit ephemeral pulses of zooplankton productivity, as the larvae must begin exogenous feeding within a few days of hatching. During the initial post-hatching phase, the prolarvae remain largely passive, relying on yolk reserves while their visual and foraging systems develop.

Lifespan estimates for Atlantic Spanish mackerel suggest that individuals can survive for up to 10 years [am = up to 10 years] under natural conditions, with the maximum longevity determined from tag-recapture studies conducted at water temperatures averaging 24.1 °C [T = 24.1 °C]. This relatively extended lifespan, compared to smaller coastal scombrids, allows repeated annual spawning bouts across multiple breeding seasons. Older, larger females contribute disproportionately to population fecundity due to their greater body mass and correspondingly higher egg production. Natural mortality remains high during the juvenile phase, but once individuals surpass the pubertal length threshold, annual survival increases substantially, enabling the species to maintain stable population densities across its range.

The species exhibits strong fidelity to warm-water habitats throughout its life cycle, with spawning aggregations forming when surface temperatures reach 24 °C or higher. The maximum daily reproductive rate of approximately 5754 eggs per individual [Ri = approximately 5754 eggs per individual] is achieved only under optimal thermal and foraging conditions, highlighting the tight coupling between environmental temperature and reproductive output in this batch-spawning species. Comparative studies within the genus Scomberomorus reveal that Atlantic Spanish mackerel occupies an intermediate position in terms of both ultimate size and fecundity, with its life history strategy emphasizing high early growth rates and protracted annual spawning seasons. Management efforts increasingly incorporate these temperature-dependent life history parameters when predicting population responses to climate variability.
